title: The burning house (Kern ch. 3)
hook: a father lures his children from a burning house with promises of carts, then gives them the finest cart

segments.voice: Yesterday, ekayana: the three vehicles were skillful means, and underneath them is one vehicle, to Buddhahood. Your line: one vehicle.

Smoke is already coming through the roof. The house is old, the beams are rotten, and there is only one door. Out in the yard stands the owner, a rich old man. Inside, his children are playing, so absorbed in their games they haven't noticed a thing. He shouts fire. They look up, puzzled, and go back to playing. They don't know what fire is. This is the parable the Buddha tells Sariputra in chapter three of the Lotus Sutra.
screen: `SMOKE THROUGH THE ROOF.` → `ONE DOOR, CHILDREN PLAYING.` → `HE SHOUTS FIRE. NOTHING.`

segments.voice: In Kern's telling, the father thinks of gathering the children in his strong arms and carrying them out. But the door is narrow, and they're running everywhere. So he tries something else. He knows what each child loves, and calls out: the toys you've always wanted are outside the door, carts drawn by goats, by deer, by bullocks. Come and get them. The children rush out together, pushing past each other, and are safe in the open air. In the yard they ask for their carts. The father gives each child the same thing, and it isn't any of the three. It's a great cart drawn by white bullocks, swift, high, decked with jewels and hung with bells, finer than anything they asked for. He is rich enough, the story says, and they're all equally his children, so why give any of them less? Now the Buddha asks Sariputra: did that father tell a lie? No, Sariputra answers. He saved their lives. Even if he'd given them nothing, he wouldn't have lied, because getting them out was the point. Then the Buddha explains. The house is the world, burning with suffering. The children are beings, absorbed in play. The three carts are the three vehicles; the great cart is the one vehicle. And the father is the Buddha, who uses skillful means because shouting the plain truth reaches no one who doesn't yet know what fire is. So here is the sutra's answer to whether shaping the message is honest: a promise made out of love, and kept more generously than anyone asked.
screen: `THE DOOR IS NARROW.` · `GOAT, DEER AND BULLOCK CARTS.` · `ONE GREAT CART FOR EACH CHILD.` · `WAS THE FATHER A LIAR?` · then, large: `OUT OF THE BURNING HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you care about who is stuck in something that isn't good for them, small or large. Notice the urge to shout fire, and set it down for a moment. Then ask what this person loves, what would make them want to walk toward the door on their own, and keep one gentle idea if it comes.
The burning house. The Lotus Sutra's parable of a father who calls his children out of a fire with the promise of carts, then gives each the finest cart of all. Today's word.
Your line: out of the burning house. Love found the way to the door. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The parable of the burning house from chapter three of the Lotus Sutra has been retold in sermons, art and study in East Asian Buddhism, as the sutra's picture of skillful means and the one vehicle.

chat.says: In the burning house story, didn't the father lie about the carts?
options: Sariputra says no: he saved their lives, then gave each child a finer cart than the ones promised.
Yes, and the sutra says the Buddha regrets it, since a teacher should never bend the truth.
No, because the carts were real, and each child got exactly the cart they wanted.
chat.meaning: In chapter three Sariputra says the father didn't lie: getting the children out was the point, and he gave more than he promised.
